Newborn Care

Foods and drinks while breastfeeding: what needs attention?

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Most foods can remain part of your diet while breastfeeding. A few substances need limits or careful checking, and some babies need an individual allergy plan. Understanding those exceptions can help you eat with confidence while protecting both your nutrition and your baby’s wellbeing.

Most foods can stay on the menu

Breast milk provides important nutrition for a growing baby, and breastfeeding usually does not require a special restrictive diet. Aim for regular meals and a range of foods that meet your own needs. Milk composition is regulated by the body, although some nutrients and exposures are influenced by what you eat and drink. A meal does not simply become an identical meal in your milk.

There are still individual exceptions, including a parent’s own allergy or a diagnosed reaction in the baby. Vegan or very restricted diets may need attention to vitamin B12, iodine and other nutrients. Babies also need their locally recommended supplement plan, particularly vitamin D; breast milk should not be described as providing every required nutrient without exception. Check the product and dose with your baby’s care team.

Choose fish by species and mercury level

Fish supplies protein and nutrients, and oily fish can provide the omega-3 fats DHA and EPA. Excess mercury can harm a developing nervous system, including learning, movement, speech and other functions. The useful response is to select suitable fish, rather than avoid all seafood or assume a single meal has caused harm.

US FDA/EPA advice for pregnancy and breastfeeding is two to three weekly servings from the Best Choices group, about 225–340 g in total. Examples include salmon, sardines and freshwater trout. The highest-mercury Avoid list includes bigeye tuna, king mackerel, marlin, orange roughy, shark, swordfish and tilefish from the Gulf of Mexico.

Species and location matter: canned light tuna is not bigeye tuna, Atlantic mackerel is not king mackerel, and Atlantic tilefish is categorised differently from Gulf tilefish. Check local fish advisories, particularly for fish caught by family or friends. If a shop label is unclear, ask which species it means before choosing.

Herbs in food are different from concentrated supplements

Ordinary culinary amounts of herbs or spices such as cumin and basil are different from medicinal teas, extracts or capsules. Breastfeeding safety information is limited for many concentrated products. Ingredients, strength, contamination and interactions with medicines can all matter, so show a pharmacist or clinician the exact label.

In the United States, supplements are regulated, but FDA does not approve them for safety and effectiveness before sale in the same way as medicines. Saying they are completely unregulated is inaccurate. A product labelled natural or sold for nursing parents is not automatically appropriate.

Herbal milk boosters are not a first-line answer to low supply. Research does not establish that every product works, nor that every study found no effect. Start with a feeding assessment, including milk transfer, feeding frequency and possible medical causes, then discuss whether any supplement has a reasonable role.

Alcohol: understand the amount and timing

Not drinking alcohol is the safest choice while breastfeeding. If you choose an occasional drink, CDC advises waiting at least two hours per standard drink before feeding. This is a practical precaution, not a guarantee of identical clearance in every person. The amount consumed, body size, food intake and time all affect exposure.

Alcohol in milk broadly follows blood alcohol levels. Levels are often highest about 30–60 minutes after drinking, and alcohol may be detectable for around two to three hours per drink, longer after more drinks. Pumping and discarding milk does not make it leave the body faster. Previously expressed alcohol-free milk can be useful if the baby needs a feed during the waiting period.

A US standard drink contains 14 g of alcohol: approximately 355 mL of 5% beer, 148 mL of 12% wine or 44 mL of 40% spirits. Definitions differ by country, and a large glass, strong beer or cocktail can contain several standard drinks. Do not use the number of glasses alone to calculate a waiting time.

Alcohol also affects feeding and safe caregiving

Alcohol is not a milk-supply remedy. It can interfere with milk release, and heavier or repeated exposure can disrupt feeding and sleep. LactMed describes short studies in which babies consumed about 20–23% less milk over several hours after alcohol exposure. That finding is not a universal or permanent 20% fall in a parent’s milk production.

Longer-term developmental concerns are a reason to avoid heavy exposure, but individual outcomes cannot be predicted from one drink. If drinking is frequent or difficult to control, ask for confidential support and an individual feeding plan rather than abruptly stopping breastfeeding without advice.

A sober adult should care for the baby whenever alcohol affects your judgement or alertness. Do not share a bed, sofa or other sleep surface with your baby after drinking. Feeding timing does not make impaired caregiving safe. Expressing may relieve breast discomfort, but it does not replace time for alcohol clearance.

Count caffeine from drinks, food and medicines

Caffeine reaches milk in small amounts. Higher exposure may make some babies restless, jittery or less able to sleep, and young or premature babies clear it more slowly. Coffee, tea, cola, chocolate, energy drinks and some medicines or supplements can all contribute. A baby’s fussiness can have other causes, so look at the overall pattern.

Guidance differs: CDC describes around 300 mg a day or less as low to moderate intake, while the main NHS breastfeeding diet page recommends no more than 200 mg. Staying within 200 mg is a cautious practical approach, with less if your baby seems sensitive or your clinician advises it.

Do not assume two or three cups always fit the limit. Size, brewing method and brand change the amount. Energy products can combine substantial caffeine with other stimulants or herbs whose breastfeeding safety needs checking. Read labels and consider a lower-caffeine option rather than treating any “energy” product as a nutritional necessity.

Convenience food does not make breast milk worthless

An overall diet dominated by foods high in added sugar, salt or less helpful fats can crowd out nutrients you need. That is a reason to build satisfying, varied meals, not to ban everything processed. Frozen vegetables, canned beans, yoghurt and fortified foods are processed too and can make eating well easier while caring for a baby.

Animal studies have explored whether a mother’s diet during pregnancy and lactation influences offspring food preferences. For example, a 2007 rat study found preferences for fatty, sugary and salty foods under its experimental conditions. It cannot show that a human parent’s occasional takeaway or sweet snack determines a child’s later tastes or obesity.

Choose realistic additions such as a protein food, whole grain, fruit or vegetable rather than judging each meal as perfect or harmful. Milk remains valuable when your diet is imperfect. If access, appetite or exhaustion makes regular eating difficult, practical support is more useful than a longer list of forbidden foods.

Spices, garlic, dairy and soy are not routine exclusions

Flavours from food can influence milk, but that does not mean a baby will reject milk after garlic, onion or a spicy meal. Most parents do not need to avoid these foods. If feeding repeatedly changes after a particular exposure, discuss the pattern with a clinician or feeding specialist before cutting out several ingredients.

Dairy and soy also do not need routine removal. A small number of breastfed babies react to food proteins, but ordinary gas, unsettled behaviour or a single unusual nappy does not identify the cause. Cow’s milk protein allergy is different from lactose intolerance, and removing dairy from a parent’s diet does not remove lactose from breast milk.

A suspected allergy needs a focused plan

The Canadian Paediatric Society reports cow’s milk protein allergy in about 0.4–0.5% of exclusively breastfed infants; estimates depend on the population and diagnosis. This should not be confused with higher rates in broader infant groups or used to diagnose a particular baby. A fixed percentage for soy allergy is not a reliable reason for routine soy avoidance.

If the history suggests a reaction through breast milk, a clinician may recommend a trial removing a specific protein, sometimes dairy and soy together for particular diagnoses. Trials often last about two to four weeks, but the choice and duration depend on the condition. Record symptoms and agree in advance when to reassess and how to confirm or reconsider the diagnosis.

Dietitian support can help replace nutrients such as calcium and vitamin D. Avoid progressively excluding more foods without review. Many children later tolerate foods that previously caused problems, but reintroduction should follow a plan. Do not attempt a home challenge after a serious immediate reaction or a severe delayed reaction. Breastfeeding can often continue during the investigation.

Know which baby symptoms need medical assessment

Eczema, blood or mucus in stools, persistent vomiting or diarrhoea, constipation, hives, wheezing or poor growth can have several causes. Mucus, gas and fussiness alone are especially nonspecific; they do not prove that a parent ate the wrong food. Describe timing, feeding, wet nappies, growth and any other symptoms to the baby’s clinician.

Seek prompt advice for blood in the stool, repeated vomiting, poor feeding or a baby who seems unwell. Breathing difficulty, swelling of the tongue or mouth, collapse or a sudden severe allergic reaction requires emergency help. Repeated vomiting with pallor or marked lethargy can also be serious even without hives.

Do not wait for an elimination diet to work when a baby has urgent symptoms. Once the baby is safe, the aim is to identify the cause with the smallest necessary dietary change and a clear follow-up plan, rather than assume every symptom comes from breast milk.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Routine avoidance of dairy, soy, spices or other nutritious foods is usually unnecessary.

Fish species, caffeine amounts, alcohol timing and exact supplement ingredients matter more than broad food labels.

How BeMama can help

Keep meals manageable and ask for a feeding or dietitian review before starting several food exclusions.

When to seek help

Breathing difficulty, mouth or tongue swelling, collapse or severe vomiting with lethargy needs urgent medical help. Do not rely on a dietary trial for an unwell baby.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Choose lower-mercury fish rather than avoiding all seafood.
  • Count caffeine from every source; babies differ in sensitivity.
  • Alcohol clearance takes time, and safe caregiving is a separate requirement.
  • Herbal supplements need checking; natural does not guarantee suitable.
  • Investigate suspected allergy with a focused, nutritionally adequate plan.

Frequently asked questions

Must I stop dairy and soy while breastfeeding?

No. Most families do not need routine avoidance. A suspected reaction may justify a specific, supervised trial with a review date and a nutrition plan.

Are all kinds of tuna and mackerel high in mercury?

No. Species matter. Bigeye tuna and king mackerel are on the US Avoid list, while other types fall into different categories. Check the exact fish and local guidance.

Can I have coffee while breastfeeding?

Usually in moderation. The main NHS diet page recommends no more than 200 mg caffeine daily, while CDC uses about 300 mg or less as low to moderate intake. Count all sources and reduce further if advised or the baby seems sensitive.

Does pumping remove alcohol from milk faster?

No. Clearance depends on time and your body’s metabolism. Expressing may relieve discomfort, but does not shorten the waiting interval before feeding.

Does one glass always equal one standard drink?

No. Glass size and alcohol strength vary. US examples contain 14 g of alcohol; local definitions differ, and a strong beer or cocktail may contain more than one drink.

Does alcohol always lower milk production by 20%?

No. Short-term studies measuring lower infant milk intake cannot be turned into a fixed, permanent supply reduction for every parent. Alcohol can still interfere with feeding and is not a milk booster.

Are herbal milk boosters approved like prescription medicines?

No. US supplements are regulated differently and are not preapproved for safety and effectiveness in the same way. Check the product and begin with a feeding assessment if supply is a concern.

Does a takeaway determine my baby’s future food preferences?

No. Animal diet studies do not establish that an occasional human meal determines later tastes or weight. Focus on an overall varied diet that is practical for you.

Does gas or mucus prove a food allergy?

No. These symptoms can have several explanations. Persistent problems, blood in stools, poor growth or an unwell baby need clinical assessment before dietary restrictions.

Can I reintroduce a food once symptoms improve?

Agree on a plan with the baby’s clinician. Reassessment is important, but home reintroduction is not suitable after every reaction, especially a serious immediate or severe delayed reaction.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
